over the organization of the first four domains, in the form of
constructing national states, national territorial waters and national
airspace. The basic proposition of this article is that the ideology of
nationalism has also infiltrated the fifth domain – cyberspace – in two
ways. First, through state-led cyber-nationalism via official

symbols or history. Second, through individual communities who use

This is a well argued and objective analysis of the US, Greek, Dutch, and Israeli ministries of
foreign affairs websites. It illustrates the way information is articulated, circulated and
disseminated through official channels and networks. The use of content analysis is possibly
adequate to the aims and goals of the article as it stresses the choice of specific sets of news
against other news. This selective process is connected with the creation and appropriation of
networks that the author adequately defines as "the nationalisation of the cyberspace".
Some important aspects are, however, overlooked. Most important, could the author more clearly
show how this process of news selection and information retrieval is filtered through those kinds
of topics that aliment the ongoing process of splintering the Internet?
Most importantly, I believe the author should emphasise how more cooperative, international and
global agendas are ignored in favour of parochial, sectional, regional and state-led agendas that
clearly reflect the respective foreign ministries' interests and visions as they are articulated in the
analysed websites.
Consequently, the author may need to ask how far crucial security threats, such as the climate
emergency, are relegated to the background insofar as they do not fit the nationalist agenda.
This is, in turn, linked to one question: what main foreign policy issues are selected for diffusion
and why? The content analysis should also reveal how some of the websites deliberately ignore
such global news and emergencies in favour of oblivion and, often, denial.
The author mentions national control of the recognised maritime space: In fact, the United
Nations’ Law of the Sea Convention (UNCLOS) for the management of marine natural resources
should be connected to the way nationalism is unable to tackle global issues, such as biodiversity
loss. The very way that natural gas and oil reserves discovered in the respective continental
shelves are rebranded is more indicative of the presence of ‘resource nationalism’ - a term that
should be better linked to the notion of "nationalization of cyberspace".




On the other hand, the author presents good evidence in the way the four ministries' websites are
nationalistically captured resulting in a "nationalization of cyberspace" against the original
cosmopolitan dream of the Internet as a neutral arena of international communications.
Accordingly, the four foreign ministries are active promoters and prominent actors in the broader
propagation of the splintering of the cyberspace into tightly bound national areas.
But this should be understood in a very broad sense, both as the propagation of ‘hot’ nationalism
in regions characterised by persisting and deeply rooted national conflicts and as forms of "banal
nationalism" in more ordinary everyday settings (as described by Michael Billig 1995).
Also, the notion of cyberspace needs to be situated with more precision according to which
components or elements are privileged in each case. I think this could be resolved by adding a few
sentences that could clarify the conceptual reach of the term and identify its components. Among
the layers that needs to be added are autonomous forces, such as those arising in the diasporas in
the process elsewhere identified as “irresponsible radicalisation”. By briefly considering this
important aspect beyond official websites, the evidence of the ongoing nationalization process
could be more nuanced and further clarified. Beyond official government and ministries websites,
Facebook’s role in inciting or assisting nationalist violence has also been studied in recent
research.
In conclusion, while the notion of “nationalization of cyberspace” is very promising, it needs to be
supplemented by a short discussion about the broader process of autonomous radicalisation,
which within the diasporas does not appear to be necessarily connected to the propaganda efforts
of the ministries of foreign affairs. The author also needs to consider how crucial security threats
at the global level such as climate change have been often ignored in most of these official
websites at least until recently. This could clarify how the "nationalisation of cyberspace" acts in
practice against the very security, interests, and survival of nations.
Minor revisions required.
References
1. Billig M: Banal Nationalism. Sage Publishing. 1995.

This article examines websites of Greek, Dutch, US and Israeli ministries of foreign affairs through
content analysis. It outlines how the websites are structured, how the missions and visions of
foreign ministries are defined and what the main foreign policy issues are. More importantly,
through the content analysis of the four foreign ministry websites, the author unpacks how each
official state website constructs and propagates its own nationalist ideology. These sections are
informative and well-organized.
I have, however, concerns over the conceptual framework, and thus methodology. The author
presents the use of national ideology in the official state websites as evidence of “nationalization
of cyberspace” and argues that this “contradicts the original purpose of the Internet as a
liberating, post-national medium, offering new forms of community”.
The conceptualization and measurement of nationalization of cyberspace needs to be well-




situated in the literature and better developed. To be more specific, can the propagation of the
national ideology in the institutional websites of foreign ministries be really considered as
‘nationalization of cyberspace’? After all, the concept of cyberspace is a term broader than
Internet. It includes physical, logical and cyber-persona layers. Physical network refers to the
machines – such as the computers, routers, cables, servers, cellphone towers, and satellites – that
establish the mechanical and electrical, magnetic, and optical lines of communication. Logical
network refers to the logical instructions and software that operate communications traffic, such
as domain name system (DNS) and Internet service providers (ISP). And finally cyber-persona or
social layer refers to the sphere through which videos, images, sounds, and texts circulate.
When author refers to the nationalization of cyberspace, which layer does he refer to? Since the
article only focuses on the official websites, it seems to refer to social layer or what in the military
realm is referred to as strategic communications. But even within this limited layer, the evidence
provided fails to denote nationalization of strategic communication/social/cyber-persona layer. In
order to arrive at such a conclusion, one needs to see further evidence of nationalization attempts,
such as a concerted effort in social media networks that propagate same or similar ideas or
positions outlined in the foreign ministry websites, use of computational propaganda or nationspecific information control policies that are in line with the national ideology dispersed in the
official websites such as filtering, surveillance, legal regulations regulating the dissemination of
information online, content control, etc.
In the literature, nationalization of cyberspace generally refers to a shift from laissez-faire and
market-oriented approaches towards the state-directed controls and regulations. Although such a
trend is also visible in Western liberal democracies, it is more prevalent among those cybersovereignist states such as China and Russia, which try to eradicate the borderless nature of
cyberspace by controlling all of these three layers through constructing underwater
communication networks, various forms of information control and data localization policies as
well as attempting to shape international cyberspace governance regimes. Nationalization of
cyberspace thus refers more of demarcating new boundaries in national cyberspace generally for
security purposes through implementing cyberspace regulations, internet policies, cyber laws and
other regulatory frameworks, thereby giving rise to a ‘splinternet’.
I therefore consider that the use of “nationalization of cyberspace” as a central conceptual
framework may not be appropriate. I suggest reframing the article centering on the reproduction
of nationalism or national identities through governmental websites, rather than nationalization
of cyberspace.

Conclusions

This article has focused on the nationalization of cyberspace
through state-led institutionalized practices. It has argued
that the ideology of nationalism has shaped our perceptions
of space and this has had implications in perceiving a new
form of space – cyberspace – along national lines. The nationalization of space process – so successful in ideologically charging real spaces – managed to expand online to cyberspace.
Cyberspace has become thus a field where nationalisms
lay claims upon, flourish, are reproduced and frequently clash.
The article further analyzed the websites of the ministries of
foreign affairs of four countries – Greece, the Netherlands,
the USA and Israel – in order to examine how current state
national ideology infiltrates cyberspace through them. All sites
reproduce intrinsic elements as well as symbolic constituent
components of their respective national identities online. The
Greek website reflects the fixation of Greek nationalism with
the past, the troubled relationship with the Greek significant
‘other’ – Turkey – and interprets the ‘national’ issues along
Greek national lines. The Dutch website reproduces the antinational, corporatist, tolerant and pluralistic traits of Dutch
national identity, while the US website reflects the sense of
mission and liberalism that have shaped American nationalism. Finally, the Israeli website echoes the Jewish national
narrative regarding the claim to the land and propagates the
Jewish national positions with regards to the conflict with the
Palestinians.
Thus, the digital avatars of the ministries of foreign affairs
of these countries seem to align with the dictates of their
official state-led national ideology. In this way, national
ideology infiltrates cyberspace, stamping it as distinctively
national. The incorporation of cyberspace to the ‘national’
space seems to have been absolute since real space national
practices – like war practices and national commemoration
practices – are being adapted to cyber-spatial characteristics.
The terminology already established – cyber-attacks, cyber-wars,
cyber-defence, etc. – corresponds to the one used for real
space national practices and seems to indicate the fact that
cyberspace has embraced nationalism.
